title: Question 9
stem:
A simple transformer is illustrated in Fig. 9.1.

{{figure:figure_9_1}}

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: State why the transformer has an iron core, rather than having no core.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what has to travel from the primary coil to the secondary coil for the transformer to work, and what would happen to it in air compared to in iron.
parts.proper_answer: The iron core guides the magnetic flux so that almost all the flux produced by the primary links the secondary, reducing loss of magnetic flux.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What links the two coils?**
Think of the primary coil as creating magnetism when current flows in it. For anything to happen in the secondary coil, that magnetism - the magnetic flux - must reach it. In air much of the flux spreads out and is lost.

Step 2: **Why iron helps**
Iron is easily magnetised and conducts magnetic flux very well. It provides a low-reluctance path that concentrates the field inside the core and carries it round from one coil to the other, so flux linkage is maximised and efficiency is high.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Explain why the core is laminated.

markscheme_points.text: (so that) heating of core is red

hints: Hint 1: Remember the core itself is a conductor sitting in a changing magnetic field - what does Faraday's law say will be induced inside the iron itself?
Hint 2: Think how cutting the solid iron into thin insulated layers changes the loops that current can flow in, and what less current means for $I^2R$ heating.
parts.proper_answer: The changing flux induces eddy currents in the core. Laminating the core into thin insulated sheets increases resistance to these currents, reducing their size and so reducing power loss by heating of the core.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Unwanted currents in the core**
The core is metal and experiences the same changing magnetic flux as the coils. By Faraday's law an e.m.f. is induced in the iron itself, driving circulating currents called eddy currents.

Step 2: **Why this wastes energy**
These eddy currents do no useful job. They dissipate power as heat in the resistance of the iron ($P = I^2R$), warming the core and lowering transformer efficiency.

Step 3: **How laminations fix it**
Splitting the core into thin laminations separated by insulating layers breaks up the large loops. The resistance to the eddy paths is greatly increased, so the eddy current is much smaller and the heating loss is greatly reduced.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: By reference to the action of a transformer, explain why the input to the transformer is an alternating voltage, rather than a constant voltage.
hints: Hint 1: Start at the input - what kind of current does an alternating voltage drive in the primary, and what kind of magnetic field does that current produce?
Hint 2: Recall Faraday's law - is it flux or change of flux that induces an e.m.f. in the secondary coil?
Hint 3: Compare this with what would happen if the input were constant after switch-on - what would the flux do then?
parts.proper_answer: The alternating input voltage produces an alternating current in the primary, producing an alternating magnetic flux in the core. This changing flux links the secondary coil, so by Faraday's law a continuously induced alternating e.m.f. appears at the output. A constant voltage would give only a steady flux, so no e.m.f. would be induced.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Alternating current makes alternating magnetism**
An alternating input voltage drives an alternating current in the primary coil. That current continuously reverses, so the magnetic flux it produces in the iron core is also alternating - constantly changing magnitude and direction.

Step 2: **Changing flux links the secondary**
The iron core carries this changing flux round to the secondary coil, so the magnetic flux linkage $N\Phi$ of the secondary is continuously changing.

Step 3: **Faraday's law gives the output**
By Faraday's law, e.m.f. is induced only when flux linkage changes: $$E = -\frac{\Delta(N\Phi)}{\Delta t}$$ So the changing linkage induces a continuous alternating e.m.f. in the secondary. With a constant d.c. input there would be a steady current and steady flux after the initial switch-on, so $\Delta(N\Phi)/\Delta t = 0$ and no output e.m.f. is induced.
